summary: Specifies how peers use Kerberos version 5 technology under the Generic Security Service API, so applications can use Kerberos through the common programming interface. It is on the standards track as a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: A single security doorway for programs, and behind it a ticket system that proves who you are. This note says how the two connect.

subtitle: How GSS-API programs carry Kerberos version 5 tickets, per-message protection and names, byte by byte.

tldr.problem: Applications that use the Generic Security Service API need a concrete, interoperable definition of how Kerberos V5 plugs in as a mechanism behind that API.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines token formats for context setup, message integrity (MIC), message wrapping and context deletion, plus name types, credential handling, status codes and quality-of-protection values.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists RFC 4121 and RFC 6649 as updating it. Its DES-based algorithms are old, and the RFC itself notes the MD2.5 algorithm may be significantly weaker than DES MAC MD5.

today: RFC 1964 is a Proposed Standard from June 1996. According to the unit metadata it has been updated by RFC 4121 and RFC 6649, so those should be read alongside it.

sections.title: What the Mechanism Defines
sections.content:
RFC 1964 specifies how peers using the Generic Security Service API (GSS-API, RFCs 1508 and 1509) work when the underlying technology is Kerberos Version 5 (RFC 1510). It covers the protocol-visible parts needed for interoperability: the tokens that peers exchange, name types, credentials, and parameter values.

The data exchanged between an endpoint and the Kerberos KDC is not specific to GSS-API, so it stays in RFC 1510. The mechanism is identified by an Object Identifier. Until advancement to Proposed Standard it used {iso(1) org(3) dod(5) internet(1) security(5) kerberosv5(2)}; afterwards it is {iso(1) member-body(2) United States(840) mit(113554) infosys(1) gssapi(2) krb5(2)}.
sections.eli5: It is the instruction sheet that lets a general security helper work with one particular ticket system.

sections.title: Context Establishment Tokens
sections.content:
The first token is wrapped in an InitialContextToken with the mechanism identifier. Inside is a Kerberos KRB_AP_REQ message preceded by a two-byte TOK_ID of 01 00. This framing applies to all tokens from the mechanism: KRB_AP_REP uses 02 00 and KRB_ERROR uses 03 00.

The authenticator carries an optional sequence number, and its checksum field conveys channel binding, service flags and optional delegation information. The checksum type is 0x8003 and its value is at least 24 bytes: a 4-byte length (hex 10 00 00 00), a 16-byte MD5 hash of the channel bindings, and 4 bytes of flags. When delegation is active, a forwardable TGT travels in a KRB_CRED message after those fields.

Without the mutual-authentication request, the exchange is one-way and the target sends nothing back. With it, the target replies with a KRB_AP_REP or a KRB_ERROR. The sequence number in the AP-REP must be included.
sections.eli5: The first message is like showing your ticket at the gate with a note saying what services you want. If you ask for proof the gate is genuine too, the gate answers back.

sections.title: Per-Message Tokens
sections.content:
After setup, two kinds of token protect data. A MIC token from GSS_GetMIC() is separate from the data and lets the receiver verify its integrity. A Wrap token from GSS_Wrap() carries the data itself, optionally encrypted, plus the integrity header. A context deletion token from GSS_Delete_sec_context() closes the context.

The headers share a layout: TOK_ID (01 01 for MIC, 02 01 for Wrap, 01 02 for deletion), SGN_ALG, a filler, the 8-byte SND_SEQ and the 8-byte SGN_CKSUM. Wrap adds SEAL_ALG and the data.

The SGN_ALG values are 00 00 for DES MAC MD5, 01 00 for MD2.5 and 02 00 for DES MAC. For Wrap, SEAL_ALG is ff ff for none and 00 00 for DES. Tokens carry no length field; the application must frame them.
sections.eli5: A MIC is a tamper-proof seal stuck on a letter you send separately. A Wrap is a sealed, scrambled envelope with the letter inside.

sections.title: Checksums, Sequence Numbers and Padding
sections.content:
Checksums cover the data, prepended by the first 8 bytes of the token header, which ties the data to the token type and algorithm. DES MAC MD5 takes an MD5 hash and then a DES-CBC MAC of it. MD2.5 uses half of the MD5 output, with a key made by reversing the bytes of the context key. The RFC says this algorithm is fairly novel and may be significantly weaker than DES MAC MD5. DES MAC may not be present in all implementations.

The 8-byte sequence number is the sender's four-byte counter followed by four direction-indicator bytes (hex 0 for the initiator, FF for the acceptor). It is DES-CBC encrypted with an IV taken from the checksum, so a spliced checksum and sequence number are detected and reflected packets are caught by the direction indicator.

Replay and out-of-sequence detection are optional. For Wrap, data is padded to a multiple of 8 bytes, with an 8-byte random confounder prepended, and encrypted with DES-CBC using the context key XORed with f0f0f0f0f0f0f0f0.
sections.eli5: Each message gets a numbered stamp that only the two sides can read, so a copied or replayed message gets spotted. The text is also padded so it fits neat 8-byte boxes.

sections.title: Name Types and Object Identifiers
sections.content:
Section 2 lists the name types accepted by GSS_Import_name(). Mandatory forms are the Kerberos principal name (components separated by /, an optional @ and realm, with \ as the quoting character), the host-based service name in the form service@hostname, and the exported name object form.

For host-based names, the hostname is canonicalized with a DNS lookup, or used as given if the lookup fails, and mapped to lower case. Optional forms are the user name, machine UID and string UID forms, whose interpretation is OS-specific.
sections.eli5: Names come in a few agreed shapes, like street addresses written in standard order, so everyone reads them the same way.

sections.title: Credentials and Parameters
sections.content:
Kerberos uses different credentials for initiating and accepting contexts. A client gets a ticket-granting ticket (TGT) and session key at login; a service's key, typically in a key table, is used for accepting. If a service needs initiating credentials that are not in a cache but has its key in a key table, the mechanism should request a TGT from the KDC and decrypt the reply with the service key.

Section 4 recommends symbolic minor status codes, such as GSS_KRB5_S_KG_TGT_MISSING. Quality of protection values are 1 (partial MD5), 2 (DES MAC of MD5) and 3 (DES MAC) for integrity, and 0 (DES) for confidentiality. Implementations must accept buffers of at least 16 Kbytes.
sections.eli5: People and services hold different kinds of keys, and the rules say which key to use for asking and which for answering.

fields.name: SEAL_ALG
fields.desc: ff ff for none, 00 00 for DES.

fields.name: SGN_CKSUM
fields.desc: Checksum of the plaintext padded data.
